title: Pauri 27, meaning: the house where all sing
hookLine: what is that door where you sit and care for all? Wind, water, fire and countless beings sing there (Japji 27)

cards: Sit outside at dawn and listen. First it seems quiet. Then the birds, dozens of them, each with its own tune.
Wind in a tree. Water somewhere, a gutter, a sprinkler. A far-off truck, a dog, a door.
After a few minutes it doesn't sound like noise anymore. It sounds like an orchestra tuning up. Pauri 27 asked what that door is like, where the One sits and cares for all.
Its answer isn't a description of a building. It's a sound.

teach.b: Pauri 27 answers with music, in paraphrase. There, countless instruments play, and countless are the players. So many ragas, the melodies of Indian music, and so many singers.
Who's singing? The elements first. In the original: gaavahi tuhano paun paanee baisantar.
Wind, water and fire sing to You. Then, in paraphrase: the king of dharma sings at Your door, and the recorders who write down every deed. Shiva, Brahma and the goddess sing.
Indra sings, among the gods. The siddhas, the celibates, the truthful, the contented, the brave warriors. The pandits and the sages with their Vedas, age after age.
The continents and worlds and universes. Those who please You, Your devotees, steeped in Your love. And so many others sing that I can't even think of them all, Nanak says.
Look at that list: wind and fire, gods whose names Guru Nanak's hearers knew, scholars and warriors, whole worlds and universes. Every one is singing to the same One. Nobody is outside the choir.

teach.h: HE IS, HE IS, FOREVER TRUE.
teach.b: Then the stanza settles, in paraphrase: He is, He is, forever true, the true Master, true His Name.
He is, and will be, and won't pass away. Whatever pleases Him, He does; no one can give Him orders. He is the King, the King of kings, and Nanak says: live within His will.
So yesterday's door opens onto a sound, and the list is wide enough that an ordinary morning could fit inside it.

how: Pauri 27 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib, and a version of it is sung in the evening as So Dar in Rehras Sahib; in gurdwaras, kirtan, sung praise with instruments, echoes its picture of the whole creation singing.

o: the instruments played in a gurdwara
the verses, or stanzas, of a hymn

games.q: who sings at the door — tap the pairs.

s: Pauri 27 describes the divine house as a silent building
it answers with music: countless instruments, players and singers.
in Pauri 27, wind, water and fire sing
Pauri 27 leaves the gods out of the choir
Shiva, Brahma, the goddess and Indra all sing; nobody is outside.

games.q: you step through the door of Pauri 27. what do you find?
o: countless beings, elements and worlds, all singing.
a single judge on a throne.
games.why: countless instruments, countless singers: wind, water, fire, gods, sages, worlds and devotees, all singing to the One.

practice: Close your eyes and listen to whatever is around you: traffic, a fan, the hum of the fridge, your own breath, a voice in another room. Instead of sorting sounds into good and bad, hear each one as its own voice in the choir.
Let nothing be noise for a while.

wordCard.voice: Ragas, the melodies of Indian music. At that door, countless instruments play, and so many ragas; wind, water and fire, gods, sages and whole worlds sing. He is, forever true.

orig.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 27: wind, water and fire sing to You.

carryVoice: Your line: everything is singing. The choir is bigger than anyone could list. Day two hundred eight, done.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6 (Japji, Pauri 27, the singers and the closing lines)
